subject: feat(transforms): read unknown partition and sort transforms (v3) (#1463)
body:
* feat(transforms): read unknown partition and sort transforms (v3)

The v3 spec requires readers to load tables whose partition specs or sort
orders use transforms the implementation doesn't recognize, and to ignore
those partition fields when filtering. Previously ParseTransform returned
ErrInvalidTransform for any unrecognized string, so unmarshalling such
metadata failed outright.

- Add an UnknownTransform type that carries the original transform string,
  reports a string result type, and projects to nil so scans don't prune on
  it. ParseTransform now returns it for unrecognized strings; malformed known
  transforms (e.g. bucket[0], overflow) still error.
- Reject committing a partition spec that uses an unknown transform via
  validateTransform, matching the spec's writer restriction.
- Keep filter expressions strict: an unknown transform in an expression term
  is still rejected, since it can't be evaluated.
- Propagate the ParseTransform error in UpdateSpec.partitionField instead of
  discarding it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* PR comments

* PR comments

* PR changes

* bucket changes

* lint error

* Address review: render unknown-transform values, guard delete writes

Blocking fixes from the round-3 review:

- UnknownTransform.ToHumanStr/ToHumanStrType render the partition value
  instead of the transform name, matching Java's Transform#toHumanString
  default (UnknownTransform does not override it). Returning the name was
  constant per spec field, so PartitionToPath produced identical keys for
  distinct partitions -- collapsing rolling-writer output and skewing
  partition-summaries/changed-partition-count.
- positionDeleteRecordsToDataFiles now rejects specs with unknown
  transforms, checking the historic specs the targeted data files were
  written under, not just the current one. Applies to both the v2 fanout
  and v3 deletion-vector paths.

Also:

- MarshalText and validateTransform reject the zero-value
  UnknownTransform, which would serialize as "transform": "".
- validateDataFilesToAdd guards AddDataFiles/ReplaceDataFiles.
- GeneratePartitionFieldName requires an explicit name for an unknown
  transform rather than synthesizing one with brackets in it.
- SortOrder.Field returns a defensive copy, like Fields.
- Clarify that CanTransform is unverifiable, and move the UpdateSpec
  rejection rationale into the NewUpdateSpec doc comment.

Tests: PartitionToPath with distinct values, UnknownTransform.Equals,
empty-name rejection, decodeTerm rejection, a mixed bucket+unknown spec
projection, a PlanFiles no-pruning test contrasted against identity, and
write rejection (AddFiles/AddDataFiles/WriteRecords/Delete) across format
versions 1, 2, and 3.

subject: fix(table): fail commits with delete-file removals instead of replaying (#1784)
body:
* fix(table): fail commits with delete-file removals instead of replaying

Delete-file removals (the deleteFilesToRemove argument of
Transaction.ReplaceFiles, and the ref-keyed deletion-vector
supersession performed by v3 merge-on-read deletes) are resolved
against the snapshot the writer built on — removal identity is
snapshot-relative. If such a commit hit a CAS conflict and went
through doCommit's refresh-and-replay, a concurrent replacement could
be inherited from the fresh base while the stale removal replays as a
no-op (checkRemovedFiles deliberately treats a superseded entry as
absent), stranding two live deletion vectors on one data file — which
the v3 spec forbids — or silently discarding a peer's delete against
a data file the replay removes.

Snapshot producers now mark the transaction non-replayable when the
staged snapshot carries delete-file removals (path-keyed delete files
or ref-keyed deletion vectors); on ErrCommitFailed the commit fails
immediately instead of entering refresh-and-replay. The caller must
re-resolve the removal against the current snapshot and try again.
Data-file removals stay replayable: they are path-keyed and the retry
rebuild already fails terminally when the path is gone from the fresh
base.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* fix(table): address review feedback on no-replay removals

Annotate the fail-fast error so callers can distinguish "refused to
replay snapshot-relative removals" from an exhausted retry budget
(errors.Is on ErrCommitFailed is preserved), clarify in the
CommitNumRetriesKey doc that recovery requires a new transaction on a
reloaded table, and pin that a no-replay conflict leaves the
transaction retriable rather than latched as committed.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* docs(table): deduplicate the no-replay rationale

The snapshot-relative-removal argument was repeated at four sites.
Keep the full explanation at the producer flag site (where the
decision is made and checkRemovedFiles lives) and the user-facing
CommitNumRetriesKey doc; the commitOpts field, the doCommit early
return, and the Transaction field now state the mechanism and point
there.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

subject: feat(table): RowDelta.RemoveDeletes for deletion-vector supersession (#1785)
body:
* feat(table): add Positions iterator to RoaringPositionBitmap

RoaringPositionBitmap exposes Set, Contains, and Cardinality but no way
to enumerate the positions it holds. Consumers that need the contents
of an existing deletion vector (e.g. to merge it into a superseding DV,
as the v3 spec requires when a data file's DV is replaced) currently
have to Serialize() the bitmap and re-parse the Iceberg portable wire
format by hand.

Add Positions() iter.Seq[uint64], yielding every set position in
ascending 64-bit order. The yielded values are the same ones passed to
Set, mirroring Java's RoaringPositionBitmap#forEach.

Tests cover the empty bitmap, a single position above the 32-bit
boundary, ascending order across multiple bitmap keys with agreement
against Cardinality, and early termination by the consumer.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* feat(table): support deletion vector supersession in RowDelta

The v3 spec allows at most one live deletion vector per data file. A
writer adding a DV for a data file that already carries one must write
a DV containing the previous DV's positions and remove the previous DV
entry in the same snapshot. Java's RowDelta supports this through
removeDeletes; the Go RowDelta could only add delete files, forcing
consumers into a two-snapshot ReplaceFiles + RowDelta workaround whose
intermediate snapshot briefly resurrects the previously deleted rows.
The engine-internal merge-on-read delete path already supersedes DVs
this way (writePositionDeletesForFiles); this exposes the same
capability to library users who write their own deletion vectors.

Add RowDelta.RemoveDeletes(files ...iceberg.DataFile), mirroring Java's
RowDelta#removeDeletes, restricted to deletion vectors. Removal
identity is (file path, referenced data file), not path alone: a
multi-blob Puffin file legally carries DVs for several data files under
one path, one manifest entry each, and superseding one blob must not
drop its siblings' entries. The snapshot producer's existing
removeDeletionVector plumbing already keys removals this way, so only
the matching entry is recorded as DELETED while other live entries at
the same Puffin path survive.

Commit first resolves every removed file to its live entry in the
current snapshot's delete manifests — when several live entries share
the removed file's path, its referenced data file selects among them,
and the removal is rejected as ambiguous if it does not identify
exactly one — then validates against the RESOLVED entries, never the
caller's copies, so a stale or forged DataFile with a real path but a
wrong referenced_data_file cannot pair a removal with an unrelated
replacement:

  - every resolved entry must be a DV (Puffin pos-delete with
    referenced_data_file); expunging plain pos/eq-delete files remains
    the rewrite path's job,
  - every removed DV's referenced data file — as recorded by the live
    entry — gets a replacement DV among the added delete files, so a
    delta cannot silently resurrect rows (content coverage stays the
    writer's responsibility, as in Java),
  - a removed file that does not resolve to a live delete entry is an
    error, as are two removals resolving to live entries that reference
    the same data file (the producer keys DV removals by referenced
    data file, and two live DVs on one data file is a spec violation to
    surface, not paper over); the DELETED record is produced from the
    manifest's own entry so it keeps its spec ID, partition, and
    sequence numbers. Blob offset and size are not part of the
    identity: the spec's one live DV per data file makes (path,
    referenced data file) unique among live entries, and every produced
    record comes from the live entry, so stale caller-side offsets are
    harmless.

When removals are present the delta commits through the overwrite
producer, which already drops removed entries from inherited delete
manifests and records them with status DELETED; the overwrite
producer's default conflict validator is suppressed in favor of
RowDelta's own, the same way rewrites do. Without removals the
fast-append path is unchanged.

Also correct the stale comments on commitOpts.validators and RowDelta
claiming pre-flight validators run only on the first attempt; doCommit
runs them on every attempt of the retry loop against the freshly
refreshed catalog state.

The end-to-end test builds a v3 table with a live DV, commits a
superseding RowDelta, and asserts single-snapshot shape (operation
delete, added and removed delete file counts), exactly one live DV
with the superseded entry marked DELETED, and row visibility at plan
level (the scanner plans only the replacement DV and its bitmap hides
the union of positions) and through materialized Arrow records. A
shared multi-blob Puffin test supersedes one of two DVs sharing a
Puffin path and asserts the sibling entry stays live (its rows still
hidden) alongside the DELETED record for the same path, plus
superseding both blobs in one delta. Validation failures are covered
for a missing replacement, a non-DV live entry behind a DV-shaped
caller copy, a forged reference targeting an unrelated DV, stale
caller metadata pairing correctly per the live entry, ambiguous and
unmatched shared-path removals, duplicate removals, an unknown file,
and an empty table.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* docs(table): pin Positions iteration-safety semantics

Document that RoaringPositionBitmap.Positions captures the key set up
front while consulting each bucket lazily, so the bitmap must not be
mutated during iteration — consistent with the rest of the type, which
is not safe for concurrent use.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* fix(table): address review feedback on RowDelta DV supersession

Close the converse validation gap: the delta validated that every
removed DV has a replacement among the added delete files, but not
that every added replacement's data file has its live DV removed. A
supersession delta could add a replacement DV for a data file whose
live DV was not in RemoveDeletes, committing two live DVs on that
file — a v3 spec violation that scan planning then rejects. The
manifest walk the removals already perform now also collects every
live DV whose referenced data file gets a replacement in this delta,
and validation requires each to be among the resolved removals.
Deltas without removals do not pay for (or get) this check; plain
AddDeletes stays unvalidated, matching Java, and is called out as
follow-up work. The same pass also rejects two added replacement DVs
referencing one data file — guaranteed corruption regardless of
removals — and detects tables already corrupted with duplicate live
DV entries, both at one Puffin path (where the producer would
tombstone every matching entry while the summary counts one removal)
and across distinct paths (where the sibling duplicate would survive
next to the replacement).

Also from review:

  - a removal-only delta now reaches the replacement-required error
    instead of failing the empty-delta guard with a message that never
    mentions removals,
  - removals require format version >= 3 up front, instead of failing
    resolution with a confusing does-not-belong lookup error on v2,
  - a live Puffin DV entry without a recorded referenced data file
    gets its own error instead of being reported as a non-DV,
  - RemoveDeletes documents that a single live entry at the removed
    path is selected regardless of the caller copy's reference (the
    reference only disambiguates shared paths), and both RemoveDeletes
    and Commit document that removal-carrying commits are
    non-replayable: a CAS conflict fails with ErrCommitFailed and the
    caller must rebuild against a reloaded table,
  - the post-commit validator comment no longer claims the producer is
    always fast-append.

New tests cover the surviving-live-DV rejection, duplicate
replacements for one data file, removal-only deltas, both
duplicate-live-DV corruption shapes, the v2 guard, and an end-to-end
RowDelta supersession race pinning fail-on-first-CAS-conflict with the
peer's DV as the sole survivor.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

---------

subject: fix(table): skip DELETED manifest entries in Snapshot.dataFiles (#1783)
body:
Snapshot.dataFiles read manifest entries with discardDeleted=false and
applied no status filter, so entries with status DELETED — tombstones
recording a file's removal — were yielded as if the files were still
reachable from the snapshot. Every caller wants live files only, so the
leak turned each of them into a correctness bug:

  - AddFiles' and AddDataFiles' duplicate walks reported false
    "already referenced" conflicts for paths whose previous
    incarnation was deleted, blocking legitimate re-adds,
  - the ReplaceFiles-family belong-to-table checks matched
    already-removed files, silently staging redundant re-deletes,
  - classifyFilesForDeletions' full-table branch collected
    tombstoned files as deletion candidates.

Discard DELETED entries when reading each manifest, using the manifest
reader's existing discardDeleted flag. Regression tests cover the
iterator level (ADDED and EXISTING entries are yielded, DELETED are
not, across data and delete manifests) and the caller level (a path
removed by a rewrite can be re-added without a false duplicate error).

subject: feat(metrics): add REST metrics reporter (#1236) (#1655)
body:
* feat(metrics): add REST metrics reporter (#1236)

Sixth PR of the metrics reporting framework. Implements the previously
stubbed catalog metrics endpoint:

- restMetricsReporter POSTs a ReportMetricsRequest to a table's
  POST .../tables/{table}/metrics endpoint. The send runs on a
  background goroutine detached from the caller's cancellation, and any
  error is logged and swallowed, so reporting never blocks or fails the
  observed scan/commit.
- The REST catalog combines it with the configured reporter when loading
  a table, gated on the opt-in rest.metrics-reporting-enabled property
  and on the server advertising the endpoint. It is off by default, so
  existing REST users see no new /metrics traffic.

Tests use a custom RoundTripper (no network listener) to assert the
async POST, the flattened report-type wire format, nil-report no-op, and
that Report never blocks on a slow server.

* feat(metrics): gate REST reporter on client opt-in with bounded async dispatch

- read enablement from client props only; server config cannot turn it on
- use canonical rest-metrics-reporting-enabled key, accept dotted alias
- dispatch reports on a bounded worker pool with a per-report timeout
- drop and log reports when the queue is full; drop queued reports on close
- Catalog.Close cancels in-flight reports and drains workers

* feat(metrics): bound auth, aggregate drop/failure logging, preserve context values

Address review on the REST metrics reporter:

- Bound the auth step: add optional ContextAuthManager so sessionTransport
  honors the request deadline for auth, and give the built-in OAuth
  token-refresh client a Timeout so a stalled token endpoint can no longer
  pin a worker indefinitely.
- Move drop logging off the caller's goroutine: submit only increments an
  atomic counter; a dispatcher-owned goroutine emits a single aggregated,
  rate-limited warning for drops and failures.
- Preserve caller context values (trace spans, request-scoped attributes) on
  the queued report while still detaching cancellation.
- Make dispatcher close one-shot (sync.Once + shared channel) so repeated
  Close spawns no extra waiter goroutine.
- Canonical enablement key wins when present; legacy dotted key is a fallback.
- Keep failed-report detail (which embeds the URL) at Debug; surface only
  aggregate counts at Warn.

* feat(metrics): honor server-side disable, tidy dispatcher shutdown

Enable REST metrics reporting only when the client opts in and the merged
config does not resolve the key to false, so a server override can suppress
reporting fleet-wide while never turning it on. Log skipped reporter
composition at debug, use an explicit timer in dispatcher close, and register
cleanup on the direct-construction dispatcher tests. Add advertised-endpoint

subject: feat(table): add Transaction.AssertRefSnapshotID (Java UpdateRequirements parity) (#1786)
body:
* fix(table): reject conflicting same-ref assertions and build ref requirements from the base state

Transaction.apply deduplicated assert-ref-snapshot-id requirements by
(type, ref) but silently kept the first when two assertions for the
same ref required different snapshot ids. Both can never hold against
the catalog: keeping either silently drops a check the caller
registered, so reject the pair at apply time with a named error
instead of a confusing catalog rejection. Only requirements actually
appended are validated against the staged metadata — a deduplicated
twin re-asserts base state the staged metadata has intentionally
moved past; its kept twin was validated when first added.

Snapshot producers built their assertion from the staged metadata's
current snapshot. For the second producer commit in one transaction
that is an intermediate snapshot the catalog has never seen, which
the new conflict check would correctly reject (previously masked by
dedup silently keeping the first assertion). Producers now assert the
BASE table's branch head — the catalog state the writer actually
read, and the only assertion that can hold at commit time. This
matches Java's UpdateRequirements, which accumulates one assertion
per ref built from the base table state.

RollbackToSnapshot and ExpireSnapshots built their assertions from
the staged refs the same way and are moved to base-state requirements
too; refs staged by the transaction itself (absent on the base) get
no assertion from them, since the update that created such a ref
already carries its own base-state requirement.

Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* feat(table): add Transaction.AssertRefSnapshotID for compare-and-swap commits

Metadata-only transactions (e.g. exactly-once bookkeeping that records
ingestion progress in table properties) cannot detect that the branch
changed between their read and their commit: the branch assertion
Commit builds implicitly is rewritten to the fresh head between
retries and the commit is replayed, so two such committers silently
interleave and the later one clobbers the earlier one's properties.
Expose the existing requirement so a committer can require that the
branch is unchanged from the head it read:

    func (t *Transaction) AssertRefSnapshotID(branch string) error

An empty branch defaults to the transaction's target branch; a branch
that does not exist on the base is required to stay absent. The
requirement asserts the BASE table's branch head — the same state
snapshot producers assert, matching Java's UpdateRequirements — so an
explicit requirement and a producer-built one for the same branch
collapse to one regardless of registration order. The branch is
marked pinned before the requirement becomes visible so a concurrent
Commit can never observe the assertion without its pinned status.

doCommit's refresh-and-replay must not rewrite these explicit
assertions to the fresh head between retries — the caller asked for
compare-and-swap semantics — so pinned branches are exempted from
rewriteRefSnapshotRequirements, and once the refreshed metadata shows
a pinned assertion can no longer hold the commit fails fast with
ErrCommitFailed instead of burning the remaining retries.

The empty-append test pins the workaround this API replaces: an empty
AddFiles commits a legal empty snapshot that moves the branch head
(Java newFastAppend().commit() parity), which writers can use to
serialize metadata-only commits through a producer's assertion at the
cost of an empty snapshot per commit.

* fix(manifest): infer manifest list version from writer schema

ReadManifestList selected its reader schema solely from the optional
"format-version" metadata key, assuming v1 when the key is absent. A

body:
* feat(table): allow added data files to target any registered partition spec

The snapshot producer already groups added files by their SpecID and
writes one manifest per spec, but AddDataFiles rejected any DataFile
whose spec id was not the current default, making the producer's
multi-spec add path unreachable. It also resolved each group's spec
through the sp.spec helper, which silently substitutes an empty spec on
lookup failure — a manifest whose declared spec disagrees with its
entries' partition tuples.

Validate each file's partition tuple against its own registered spec —
the shape of Java's MergingSnapshotProducer — error on unregistered
spec ids in both the validation and the producer, and iterate spec
groups in sorted order for deterministic manifest output. This lets
writers keep producing under a previous spec after a partition
evolution and lets rewrites migrate files between specs.

subject: fix(table): look up removed-file partition specs by ID (#1816)
body:
accumulateSummaryDelta resolved partition specs two different ways.
Added files went through sp.spec(int(df.SpecID())), a by-ID lookup over
GetSpecByID, while removed data files, delete files and deletion
vectors indexed the spec slice directly with specs[df.SpecID()].

Spec ID is an identifier, not a slice position. RemovePartitionSpecs
filters the slice without renumbering the survivors, and specs loaded
from metadata keep the partition-specs array order, so the two come
apart on ordinary tables. The index expression is evaluated as a call
argument, so it fails before removeFile ever runs: a Delete, Overwrite
or RewriteFiles commit that removes files panics with index out of
range, or silently attributes the change to the wrong partition when
the ID stays in bounds but points at the wrong entry.

Use sp.spec() in the three removal loops so both halves of the function
agree, and drop the now-unused local. Unknown IDs then yield an empty
unpartitioned spec instead of panicking, matching the add path.

The regression test evolves specs 0/1/2, removes spec 1 so the slice
becomes [id0, id2], then sends the same spec-2 data file down both
branches and asserts they report the same changed partition.

Fixes #1815

subject: fix(hive): jitter lock-retry waits to decorrelate contending clients (#1640)
body:
* fix(hive): jitter lock-retry waits to decorrelate contending clients

calculateBackoff is a pure function of the attempt number and the configured
bounds, so every client waiting on the same table lock computes an identical
sequence of delays. Contention is the precondition for entering the retry
loop at all, which means those clients are waiting simultaneously by
construction: they re-check the lock in lockstep and each round of CheckLock
arrives at the metastore as a burst.

The jitter is added on top of the interval rather than centred on it. Equal
jitter is the more familiar formula but it halves the wait, which would let a
caller poll sooner than the lock-check-min-wait-time they configured.

Once the sequence saturates at maxWait there is no headroom left to add into,
and that is the state a persistently contended client stays in, so leaving it
unjittered would put clients back in lockstep exactly when it matters most.
The wait is spread downwards there instead. A cap is an upper bound on the
polling interval rather than a target, so drawing below it breaks no contract.

How far down it may draw is the subtle part. Flooring at half the interval
would let the first saturated attempt wait less than the attempt before it,
since the last unsaturated interval lands in [maxWait/2, maxWait). The floor
is therefore the last interval the doubling sequence produced before hitting
the cap, which the schedule has already cleared, and which cannot fall below
minWait because that is where the sequence starts.

Reachability of the saturated path is config-gated: the defaults (100ms, 1
minute, 4 retries) top out at 800ms and never saturate, so it needs a lowered
lock-check-max-wait-time or a raised retry count.

* Keep the at-cap floor from dropping below the configured minimum

The replay loop I added in the previous commit only raises the floor while
walking intervals that are below maxWait. When lock-check-min-wait-time is
itself greater than or equal to lock-check-max-wait-time the loop never runs,
so the floor stayed at half the interval. With a 90s minimum against a 60s
maximum, calculateBackoff resolves to 60s and the spread could return 30s --
a third of the configured minimum, and the opposite of what the doc comment
promised. options.go accepts that configuration today, so it is reachable.

minWait is now applied as a floor before the replay rather than relying on the
replay to reach it. Where minWait is at or past the cap the floor exceeds the
interval and the wait is returned unspread, which is the only honest answer
when the configured minimum cannot be respected any other way.

This was a regression in my own previous commit, not a pre-existing gap.
Caught by @zeroshade in review.

Also shortened the applyJitter comment from 31 lines to the invariants, per the
same review. The removed text ended by claiming the wait could never fall below
minWait, which is precisely what it did.

Tests: a 90s/60s regression case, and an acquireLocks-level test that exercises
the call site and bounds the aggregate retry delay. The latter asserts its lower
bound tightly and its ceiling loosely, since wall-clock assertions flake on busy
CI runners.

* Use the max builtin for the at-cap floor

Same behaviour in fewer lines, and it matches how the rest of the repo spells
this: catalog/rest/scan_planning.go already uses the builtin for its retry
delay. Suggested by @zeroshade in review.

subject: fix(partitions,sort): accept ordinal source IDs when decoding (#1665)
body:
* fix(partitions,sort): accept ordinal source IDs when decoding

Decoding rejected source-id 0 in partition specs and sort orders, but
positivity is only an invariant for specs already bound to a schema.
Create-table and commit requests carry unbound specs whose source IDs
are the client's ordinal placeholders: Spark numbers the root struct's
fields from zero, so partitioning or sorting by a table's first column
sends source-id 0. Those requests failed with "source ID must be
positive: 0".

Reject only negative IDs during decoding and leave positivity to schema
binding, which is where Java enforces it. TableMetadata.newTableMetadata
assigns fresh IDs and remaps each spec field by looking the source name
up in the request schema; reassignIDs already does the same, so ordinal
IDs were handled correctly once past decoding. Non-resolvable IDs are
still caught: AddPartitionFieldBySourceID and SortOrder.CheckCompatibility
report source IDs missing from the schema.

Regression tests cover a create-table request numbered from zero through
NewMetadata and a metadata round trip, for both partition specs and sort
orders.

subject: feat(metrics): add OpenTelemetry reporter (#1236) (#1767)
body:
Seventh PR of the metrics reporting framework. Adds an in-module
metrics/otel package with an OpenTelemetry-backed reporter that maps
every field of a ScanReport's ScanMetricsResult and a CommitReport's
CommitMetricsResult to an OpenTelemetry instrument, so scan/commit
metrics can flow to any OTLP backend.

The host owns the OpenTelemetry SDK: the reporter takes a Meter from the
global MeterProvider (or one supplied via WithMeter); with no SDK
registered the instruments are no-ops. Durations are histograms (ms);
every other field is a monotonic counter (bytes carry the By unit,
counts are unit-less). By default scan metrics carry iceberg.table.name
and commit metrics carry iceberg.table.name and iceberg.operation;
iceberg.schema.id is opt-in via WithAttributes and snapshot id is never
a metric attribute. It is an in-module package rather than a separate
module because go.opentelemetry.io is already a transitive dependency.

Names, units, and the attribute set mirror Java's OtelMetricsReporter
(apache/iceberg#16250) so metrics stay consistent across
implementations; treat them as provisional until that PR merges.

subject: feat(dv): add SetRange and RunLengthEncode to RoaringPositionBitmap (#1758)
body:
Set was the only mutator, so range-shaped deletes (dead blocks or row
groups) cost one call per position and serialized as array or dense
bitmap containers. SetRange marks [start, end) with one roaring AddRange
per 2^32-position bucket, and SerializeDV now run-length encodes before
emitting bytes: 100,000 contiguous positions drop from 8235 to 49 bytes.

Mirrors Java's RoaringPositionBitmap.setRange/runLengthEncode and
BitmapPositionDeleteIndex.serialize, which run-encodes before writing.
Deviations: an inverted range is a no-op rather than an exception, and
RunLengthEncode returns nothing (roaring's RunOptimize reports nothing).

all-container-types-position-index.bin rebuilt via SetRange (132,561

subject: feat(metrics):    Instrument commits and emit CommitReport ( #1236) (#1596)
body:
* feat(metrics): instrument commits and emit CommitReport (#1236)

Fifth PR of the metrics reporting framework. Emits a CommitReport from
the commit path on successful completion:

- the retry loop in doCommit now records the total duration and the
  number of attempts;
- the committed snapshot's summary is mapped into a CommitReport, under
  Java's commit-report metric names. iceberg-go's summary keys differ
  from those names (e.g. added-files-size -> added-files-size-bytes,
  deleted-data-files -> removed-data-files, added-position-deletes ->
  added-positional-deletes); the mapping translates them so the wire
  format matches Java. Metrics with no iceberg-go summary key (DVs,
  manifest counts) are omitted rather than reported as zero.

The committed table now also preserves its reporter. With the default
no-op reporter this is a pure no-op for existing users.

* docs(metrics): note deferred CommitReport.Metadata population

Java's CommitReport carries a metadata map (engine/commit context)
that iceberg-go does not thread into the commit path yet. Mark it as
a TODO in buildCommitReport rather than emitting an empty map.

* fix(metrics): address commit report review feedback

Bracket TotalDuration to the commit loop, populate manifest metrics,
guard report emission against panicking reporters on both commit and
scan paths, skip emission on unresolved branch head, and make
attemptsUsed int64. Add retry-attempt and manifest test coverage.

subject: fix(hive): tighten the lock-jitter docs and tests from post-merge review (#1714)
body:
Follow-up to #1640, all of it raised by @laskoviymishka after approving.

On whether the downward-spread branch earns its complexity: keeping it, and the
reason is now a test. At minWait=300ms, maxWait=1s the sequence runs 300ms,
600ms, then saturates. The last uncapped interval is 600ms but d/2 is 500ms, so
the flat max(minWait, d/2) floor would let the first capped attempt wait less
than the one before it. The divergence appears whenever the ratio is not a clean
power of two, which the previously pinned 100ms/1s case could not show. Removing
the replay loop makes the new test fail with draws around 560-590ms.

The branch is genuinely unreachable on defaults, so that is now stated at the
top of it rather than left for a reader to work out.

Doc corrections:
- The invariant list claimed the result never falls below minWait. That is false
  when minWait > maxWait, and our own test pins it: the call returns exactly
  maxWait, which is below the configured minimum, because no value honours both
  bounds. Qualified rather than deleted.
- Recorded that the spread here is wider than Java's. Tasks.exponentialBackoff
  jitters by roughly 10% of the current delay; this draws from [d, 2d]. That is
  deliberate, but Go and Java clients on the same metastore spread differently
  and the next reader should not assume otherwise.

Test corrections:
- The at-cap bounds test asserted >= maxWait/2 when the guaranteed floor is
  800ms, so a regression to 600ms would have passed. Tightened, and the message
  reworded since it read as an upper bound on a GreaterOrEqual check.
- The acquireLocks test asserted wall-clock elapsed time, which sleeps every run
  and can flake on a loaded runner. It now counts CheckLock calls instead. The
  additive never-shorter property is already covered without touching the clock.

subject: fix(deps): bump twmb/avro to v1.8.0 and adapt to its API changes (#1843)
body:
v1.8.0 changes Schema.Root() to return *SchemaNode rather than SchemaNode,
which breaks four value-context uses here. Field access auto-derefs, so the
fix is a deref at the sites that pass or assign the node by value.

It also changes what integral JSON metadata decodes to. Root() now preserves
numeric precision, so a field's "field-id" property comes back as int64
where it was float64 before (integers above 2^53 previously rounded through
float64). schemaFieldID matched only int and float64, so under v1.8.0 it
returned false for every field.

That failure is silent rather than loud: getFieldIDMap ends up with an empty
map, avroEncodePartitionData iterates nothing, and partition values are
written to the manifest as null. The header schema is still correct, and the
read path drops the same keys for the same reason, so nothing errors --
partition data is just lost. Pinned by the two existing tests that catch it,
TestDataFileStatisticsDecimalPartitionManifestRoundTrip and
TestCollectDeadPositionDeletesPartitioned.

Accepting int64 alongside int and float64 keeps this working across both
avro versions.

* fix(io/gocloud): suppress transfer-manager checksum headers in compat mode

The S3 transfer manager v0.3.x sets s3.Options.RequestChecksumCalculation
per call from its own transfermanager.Options, which resolves to
WhenSupported by default. That override lands after the client-level
RequestChecksumCalculationWhenRequired we set for compat mode, so the SDK
re-added a default CRC32 checksum to uploads against custom endpoints.

Replace the SDK's AWSChecksum:SetupInputContext middleware in place for
object write inputs instead of only clearing the input algorithm ahead of
it. With no algorithm on the request context the downstream compute
middleware is a no-op, so no x-amz-checksum-* header, x-amz-trailer,
aws-chunked framing, or STREAMING- payload hash is emitted. Non-write
operations, including ones S3 requires a checksum for such as
DeleteObjects, delegate to the original middleware unchanged, and clients
without compat mode are unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(io/gocloud): clear precomputed checksum fields on compat-mode writes

Suppressing the SDK's checksum context only covers checksums the SDK
computes itself. The modeled Checksum* input fields are bound straight to
x-amz-checksum-* headers by the rest-xml serializers without consulting
that context, so caller-supplied values still reached custom endpoints.
The transfer manager copies explicit checksums into PutObject and
CompleteMultipartUpload, and ChecksumType into CreateMultipartUpload and
CompleteMultipartUpload, so this was reachable in practice.

Clear every checksum field that binds to a header across all four write
shapes, per the s3 v1.106.0 input structs and their
awsRestxml_serializeOpHttpBindings*Input serializers: the precomputed
digests (CRC32, CRC32C, CRC64NVME, MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA512, XXHASH128,
XXHASH3, XXHASH64) on PutObject, UploadPart, and CompleteMultipartUpload;
ChecksumAlgorithm on PutObject, UploadPart, and CreateMultipartUpload; and
ChecksumType on CreateMultipartUpload and CompleteMultipartUpload.
CompleteMultipartUploadInput was not handled at all before.

Per-part checksums under MultipartUpload.Parts are left intact:
awsRestxml_serializeDocumentCompletedPart writes them as XML body
elements, not headers, so they are legitimate and stripping them could
invalidate the completion request.

The clearing pass now runs for every operation instead of only inside the
swapped middleware's skip branch, because CreateMultipartUpload and
CompleteMultipartUpload register no checksum setup middleware in
s3 v1.106.0 and so were never reached by the swap.

Add regression tests for end-to-end compat-mode multipart uploads,
explicit caller-supplied checksums and ChecksumType, retention of
per-part body checksums, DeleteObjects still receiving its required
checksum, and non-compat clients still checksumming normally.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(io/gocloud): strengthen compat-mode checksum regression guards

Polish for the compat-mode checksum suppression added in the previous
commit, in response to review:

- Assert the exact multipart request mix (1 create, 3 parts, 1 complete)
  and check the headers of every captured request, not just the last, so
  a checksum leaking onto an earlier part cannot slip through.
- Require a non-nil captured header map before asserting the absence of
  checksum headers, so a request that never reached the test server can
  no longer make the assertions pass vacuously.
- Drain part bodies with io.Copy(io.Discard, ...) rather than buffering
  them, keeping the drain-before-respond behavior that avoids the client
  seeing a broken pipe on multi-megabyte parts.
- Collapse the duplicated write-shape type switches into one, so the set
  of object write operations is enumerated in a single place.
- Document that compat mode silently discards caller-supplied checksums,
  and why erroring out is not workable.

No change in suppression behavior.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(table): use tblutils alias for Enumerated in arrow_scanner

The empty-batch sentinel block added in #1537 referenced internal.Enumerated, but #1426 renamed the table/internal import alias to tblutils. The two changes merged without a textual conflict, leaving a dangling reference that fails to compile (table/arrow_scanner.go:1027:35: undefined: internal). * fix(ci): use block-style list in labeler.yml for actions/labeler v7
